utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Saxon, I have heard you have problems. You do what you choose, you want to stand you can stand; you want to sit, you can sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do stand because of exercise and not because you're objecting, indicate -- differentiate that from when you are objecting so that I can call on you when you are objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have appearances then starting with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dan Saxon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Novak Lukic and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Just for the record, the Chamber is still sitting pursuant to 15 bis, Judge David still indisposed. And good morning to you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Skrbic. I know you know this, but I must record that I've reminded you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intellectually speaking my testimony makes me happy, and I will abide by the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skrbic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us first go back to the document that we could not examine in the absence of a translation. I was just told that there is an official translation of the document, so I will call up 65 ter document of the Defence 00072D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me first identify the document for the transcript. As the heading says, it is an order determining the competence and powers of commanding officers on decision-making -- in decision-making about relations in the service of the military personnel and workers in the employ of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on we will see that the date is that of the 16th of June, 1992 and that it was signed by Bogdan Subotic. Mr. Skrbic, let us first go back to your yesterday's testimony. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I kindly ask that the transcript in English be switched on on my left monitor so that I can follow the questions as they are put. Thank you very much. Yes, I have seen this document, and I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does this order define or regulate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order signed by the then-minister of defence Bogdan Subotic, otherwise a general, determines the competence and powers of the senior officers of the Army of Republika Srpska when it comes to the relations within the service and the various powers as defined in the items designated in sequential numbers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And which are these relations that the order regulates, and I mean the relations within the service?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a concise definition of these relations would be powers in the field of defining, or rather, promoting, appointing, and transferring personnel within the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does it also regulate the termination of service?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the basis for the issuance of this order? I don't want to lead you in any way.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no need for that at all, because you can see the basis in the preamble of the document where it is stated that the basis is Article 370 of the Law on the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is pursuant to this article that the member of the government, i.e., minister of defence issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the last page now. I think that the document is self-explanatory, and I'm interested, in fact, in item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the penultimate page in English -- oh, I'm sorry, so the page before this one in B/C/S as well. This is merely the certification of the original. So the previous page in the B/C/S and in English -- yes, we have the right page. But the text continues on to the next one in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By virtue of this order what are the rights and duties of the commander of the Main Staff with regard to the relations within the service?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 6 of the order provides for the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, or rather, at the time it was called the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina provides for his power under A, and let me not explain this, that according to the peacetime organisational structure, he shall appoint active-duty, non-commissioned and commissioned officers. Then there is B where he will conclude fixed contracts; and C, pursuant to peacetime and war time assignments, he will also appoint junior officers up to and including the rank of lieutenant-colonel; and D, he shall also take decisions on layoffs and termination of active duty service -- of active duty non-commissioned and commissioned officers up to and including the rank of lieutenant-colonel; and E, promote non-commissioned and commissioned officers up to and including the rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who takes decisions for posts within the service involving the rank of a lieutenant in the VRS or lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to all these various items, let us not read them again, it's the minister of defence who will issue these decisions, also pursuant to the legislation in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have already discussed the matter involving generals and who has the power to issue such decisions for them. Let me ask you this: The order, as we have seen it now with the various powers it defines, was it in force throughout the war, that is to say up until the Dayton Accords in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, when Mr. Ninkovic took up the position of the minister of defence, what was the situation like with regard to the promotion of lieutenant-colonels and various other status related issues as defined in this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Ninkovic, the defence minister, who was a civilian, not a serviceman, issued a draft order defining powers in 1995 wherein item 6 was fully modified and the powers of the commander of the Main Staff were derogated with regard to the appointment, release from duty, and promotion of active-duty servicemen. Since this was a draft decision, we, and when I say we, Your Honours, I apologise, I have to be quite clear on this issue, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska proposed that the president should not adopt such a document and that he should not allow the minister to forward such a document to the Main Staff of the VRS. This proposal was heeded and such an order never saw the light of day because the Main Staff suggested that the president should decide, that the order that we have now on our screens from 1992, should continue to be in force, and this was the case, in fact, throughout the existence of the Main Staff of the VRS. What the situation was like later on when the General Staff of the VRS was set up is something I don't know because my service within the VRS had by that time ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted into evidence. We have an official translation, so I think we have all the requirements in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can I get clarity on that last sentence of the witness. He says, there was a case throughout the existence of the Main Staff of the VRS. What the situation was like later on when the General Staff of the VRS was set up is something I don't know because, when did this change take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will get to that, Your Honour. That's 1996. And I did intend to discuss this issue with the witness, so we will get to that topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D332. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us resume where we left off yesterday when we discussed the various appointments, and I'm sure that now we've seen this document, it will be much easier to understand documents to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up document 164D. I would, in fact, withdraw the document because I see that we don't have page 2 in e-court, so we don't have a complete document. I will, however, deal with the document later. I will withdraw it for the time being. I think that it's a known document. Can we now call up 65 ter document 00236D. That's Defence 65 ter document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what is this that we can see before us now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the Serbian version be enlarged somewhat. The English as well. That's enough, thank you. This is a copy of a document entitled "record of taking up of duty" on behalf of this individual here who is a member of the armoured units and his name is Dragan Milomir Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that this document is dated 1999, and there's a stamp in fact, or a seal at the bottom. Can we have the bottom to see who the superior officer is, who signed this transfer of duty document. Can you tell me -- it says the command of the 5th Corps, so can you tell us this stamp or seal, who does it belong to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can clearly be seen from the copy of this document that the responsible officer who signed the document was Major-General Svetozar Andric. Now, the stamp itself says that it's the command of the 5th Corps, and this is the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which through re-organisation of the VRS resulted in the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, in 1999 Major-General Svetozar Andric was commander of the 5th Corps, that's to say of which army then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, if this is a document of the VRS, why does it have Belgrade on it, 1st of February, 1999, Belgrade. And then it says, I have taken up the duties of commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade 5th Corps 30th Personnel Division. Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D333. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document I wish to show and has to do with the same matter is the OTP evidence Exhibit P2099. I think it's a public document. If we can please, the second page, so that we can see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this document and who signed it, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having examined the copy that I'm looking at, I can confirm that this is an authentic document since it was signed -- it was supposed to be signed by me, Major-General Petar Skrbic but since I was most likely absent, this document was signed pursuant to my authorisation by my deputy Colonel Martic [as interpreted] whose handwriting I can recognise. Colonel Maltic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page. The date is 13th of September, 1995, but there's some other dates mentioned there, so could you please comment on that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see here that certain persons, whose names we don't need to mention, are being transferred. You can see at the top it says that the following were being transferred to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and then their names that go on to the second page, and I was in charge of transferring these persons because I was assistant commander for organisational and personnel matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move the first page, not the second page, but the first page to the right a little bit. Can we see the handwritten annotations on the left side. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, next to the person number 2 and number 3, there are some handwritten annotations, can you comment on them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the relevant page of the English so that we can read the transcript of the handwritten annotations, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version needs to be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And now can we be guided as to where are these annotations supposed to be in the English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see the heading "Drinski Corps," Drina Corps. It's the previous page in English. Here on this page in the English version, Your Honour, you see the words "to Drina Corps," but then most likely on the next page is the rest of the text written in Cyrillic script. I can't read this in English. I will comment on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can confirm that what is written by hand in Cyrillic script has not been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then are you going to ask the witness about that part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, certainly. That's what I wanted to do. I want the witness to explain the handwritten annotation, what it means. We just needed to find the corresponding portion in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My point being that your English version is not a copy of the Cyrillic script because it doesn't have this annotation transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a P exhibit, Your Honour. A Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, talk to Mr. Saxon about that. Yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, so what does it read, this handwritten annotation in Cyrillic script, and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath the heading "to the Drina Corps" next to the person number 2, Inic Vukadin, son of Novak, somebody wrote by hand "mistake, to the HK," which stands for the Herzegovina Corps. Therefore, this person named here, was not being assigned to the Drina Corps, but rather to the Herzegovina Corps. Next to the following name, person number 3, where it says "Petrovic, Djokica, son of Cvjetko," on the left margin, there's an annotation, 5BVP, which stands for the 5th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we see the following page in the B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to the following page, can we see the top of the B/C/S page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, you are right. There is something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the top of the page there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell us what is written by hand in Cyrillic script in the upper right corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, sir, under number 04540747, there is a handwritten annotation in Cyrillic script that reads [B/C/S spoken] and that means entered into records, and then the annotation is underlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now see the second page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does it say here next to number 4, General?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to number 4, which is a person called Zekic, Milivoj, son of Matija. There is an acronym, 1BPBR, which stands for the 1st Battalion of the infantry brigade, and this notation is underlined as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, was this data written typically by hand, and if so, by whom was it done when persons were assigned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this, Mr. Lukic, and I can tell you with almost full certainty even whose handwriting this is, but I don't know if I may say that in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think there are any hindrances to that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the annotations of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I had to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me ask you this: Do you remember that in mid-July 1995, a certain number of officers of the Army of Yugoslavia arrived who were supposed to be assigned to posts in the VRS. I can even tell you that the Prosecution claims that at about 13th of July, some 30 officers of the Army of Yugoslavia arrived in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is paragraph 60C of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like to speak of the numbers because I'm not sure of the numbers, but I can confirm that a certain number of officers arrived, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether some of those officers at the time were assigned to the Drina Corps, or rather, to the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially none of the officers were assigned to the Drina Corps out of that group of officers, none were assigned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where were they assigned, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest number was assigned to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and that, Mr. Lukic, depended on their military occupational specialty. All of those who were from the air force were sent to the air force command and anti-aircraft defence. None of them were sent to the infantry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just get clarity. Mr. Skrbic, you answered a question, do you remember whether some of those officers at the time were assigned to the Drina Corps or rather this area of Srebrenica, and you said, Initially none of the officers were assigned to the Drina Corps out of that group of officers. None were assigned there. When you say "initially," what do you mean? Are you suggesting that later they were assigned to the Srebrenica area or to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, based on the documents of this Tribunal, I know that some officers from the Main Staff including Bogdan Sladojevic did go to the Drina Corps. Bogdan Sladojevic went there pursuant to an order as a representative of the Main Staff, and none of the officers were posted, were assigned to the Drina Corps at the time, at the time that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And is this Bogdan, sorry, the name is not -- surname is not sort of coming up on the screen, was he part of the officer from the army of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was an officer who had arrived with that group and we assigned him, we posted him to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But after several days we moved him, we transferred him to the Main Staff of the VRS at the request of General Jovanovic. He was assigned to his staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Rather General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can clarify something regarding colonel and later general Bogdan Sladojevic. Do you know until what time he remained in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have I understood you well, you are asking about General Bogdan Subotic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm asking about Sladojevic who later became general, Bogdan Sladojevic. Until what time did he remain in the VRS and from which army did he retire, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Sladojevic remained in the Army of Republika Srpska until it was abolished, and I think that he remained in service even after the VRS was abolished and then he retired from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "abolished," when was the Army of Republika Srpska abolished according to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of December 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a point I don't understand, I don't know whether you are interpreted correctly. You say Bogdan Sladojevic remained in the Army of Republika Srpska until it was abolished, and I think that he remained in service even after the VRS was abolished and then he retired from there. That doesn't make sense. If he remains in service, in service of which army, if the army is abolished, and where does he retire from, where is the they? Maybe you were misinterpreted, but that's what the record says. Can you correct that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not quite clear on that terminology as you are not. The VRS was abolished, however, a number of officers remained in service because a third, in brackets, Republika Srpska Regiment was set up which became part of what is, I suppose now called the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of course, that's a single armed force. So Bogdan Sladojevic remained in the service of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but please don't hold me to that because I really don't know what the proper title of that armed forces right now, and that's a single armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina comprising all the entities. I wasn't really following these developments, so please don't hold it against me if I don't give you precise data. I am a bit puzzled by it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It explains remained in service even after abolishment of the VRS. It explains that part of it. Even if we don't know the name of that army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you please comment on the following document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a Defence 65 ter document, 00066D. I would like to discuss transfers with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we can see that the document was signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander Colonel Petar Skrbic, and I do confirm the authenticity of the document because the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is self-explanatory, but can you explain to us what was involved here, who are you writing to and why?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to give you a concise answer and not burden you with details. What can be seen in the upper right-hand corner is to the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and the appointed, or rather, the named individuals Knezevic and Glisic asked for a transfer from the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment, which was stationed in Han Pijesak, and they wanted to be transferred to Banja Luka apparently because of some private reasons of their own, and this is within the VRS. The commander of the Main Staff decided to deny their request and we informed the regiment accordingly, and they were, in turn, supposed to inform the individuals concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D334. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 65 ter document 00313D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us again who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was signed by assistant commander Major-General Petar Skrbic, that's to say myself, and I confirm the authenticity of the signature, although I changed my signature for awhile, I don't know why, but this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is dated the 25th of December, 1996. Can you tell us what the procedure was with regard to this document, and how these requests for transfers to the Army of Yugoslavia were dealt with?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the requests for transfer to the Army of Yugoslavia were discussed at the meeting, the collegium meeting of the commander of the Main Staff. It was the commander who ultimately decided on such requests and for the most part they were denied. Only those requests involving individuals who were ill, seriously wounded, or had family difficulties were accepted. Otherwise the -- most of the requests were denied that I was involved with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this is late 1996. At the time what sort of a position did the commander of the Main Staff take with regard to such requests for transfers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This date marks the end of the operation of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. We were aware of it, but we were still vested with powers to regulate the various relations within the service. However, the general position that we adhered to throughout the war was that no one without showing good cause could be transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia. And we stuck by that position in order to prevent the erosion of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will discuss the events in 1996 later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit D335. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up a Defence 65 ter document 00314D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document that is very similar to the earlier one, and I think it even bears the same date, but the decision is the opposite of the earlier one. Tell us, when requests are denied by the collegium, is the procedure involved the same, would the officer concerned be informed of it or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is authentic since it bears my signature, and there's a follow-up action whether the request is approved or denied. Both the command and the individual concerned are informed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned a number, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many similar documents are we going to see?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more, Your Honours. I was really trying to give a copy each, and I am going to show another P document which is similar to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D336.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up P1858.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us see who signed this document. Can we see the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a copy of an authentic document where clearly Colonel Stojan Malcic, my deputy, signed this in my stead, and he was authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that there are two individuals listed here whose lines were circled, and we see handwritten annotations in Cyrillic. Can you tell us who wrote this annotation and why?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to the individual listed under 2, Dragutin Erak it is handwritten that he left off his own free will. And also in relation to the person listed under 3, I will not read his name aloud, I will have words to say about this. It also says that he left of his own free will and those who were thus qualified were considered deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you considered them to be deserters, did this mean that by virtue of that qualification, did you in the VRS or in the Army of Yugoslavia initiate any follow-up steps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the Army of Republika Srpska we initiated appropriate legal proceedings. The matters were handed over to the courts, but to not much avail. The courts functioned poorly be it because of the war. At any rate, the procedures were very lengthy. What such cases, what became of them, and how they were dealt with in the Army of Yugoslavia, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last sentence he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, the interpreters would like you to repeat just the last sentence, they missed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will modify this somewhat. Let me not say we, but the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska felt that their service should be terminated, that they should be discharged from service as deserters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But you were telling us about the court procedures that you took, reported them to appropriate -- you said you took appropriate legal proceedings but these were lengthy and the cases, what became of them and how they were dealt with in the Army of Yugoslavia, you don't know. And I don't know whether there was anything else you said after that which is what the interpreters wanted you to repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing else but the sentence that I said just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up Prosecution Exhibit P1860. A moment, please, I think the document has several pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not this one, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. Let me see if that's what we are looking for. Yes, this is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell me who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copy of the document that I'm looking at was signed by lieutenant-colonel Dane Maric who worked in the sector that I headed. He was also authorised to sign these documents because we couldn't be present at the command post at all time. He also drafted the document which is denoted by the DM initials on the left-hand side. DM standing for Dane Maric. And he, or rather, the sector that I headed informed the command of the Drina Corps about this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: It is clear from the document that the individual addressed the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Were there such situations, and it obviously transpires from this document that it was, that a chief or anyone else from the Army of Yugoslavia should address you with the request for an individual to be returned to the service of the Army of Yugoslavia; how many such cases were there, if any; and what was their fate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were no such requests. I have to add a minor reservation. Except for technical specialties in air force where the Army of Yugoslavia was lacking personnel and we didn't have sufficient needs for such personnel, that seems to be the only such example in my mind now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And why didn't you have the need for the technical specialty of air force during the war? Why did you have no such needs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to remind everybody in the courtroom that there was a flight ban in force at the time. Only NATO air force was allowed to fly in the air-space above Republika Srpska at that time, and they were the only ones flying throughout the war. So the air-space above the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just Republika Srpska, was controlled by NATO air force and their land-based radars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Defence document from our 65 ter list 01076D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document bears the date of your transfer to the Army of Republika Srpska when you were in the 2nd Krajina Corps. I think the document is rather clear, but rather, can we first turn to page 2 to confirm that it was signed by the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. We can see that the document was sent to the sector where you eventually transferred to in 1994 and also to all other units of the Army of Republika Srpska. On the previous page, could you please comment part of the order, item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the first page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first sentence actually explains the purpose of this order, why General Mladic issued this order. We don't need to comment on it. But let us now just look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was not drafted within the sector for organisational mobilisation and personnel affairs because at the bottom you can see the addressees and among the addressees, it is this sector as well. I assume that this document came from the administration for development and finance based on the registration number. They probably prepared this document for the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to sign it and he did sign it. And you want me to comment on the item where it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want you to comment on item 2 under the word "order."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Organs in charge of planning and MFP which stands for materiel and financial operations shall immediately send to the accounting and data processing centre of the Ministry of Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia lists of names of individuals whose entitlements are to be abolished and request that centre to stop further payment, spending issues of appropriate decisions. So if it were established that they do not meet the requirements for receiving such entitlements, then we were to inform the organs, whose names I have just read out, that they should stop any further payment of such entitlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is missing in the transcript, but we can see it in the translation in English that we are requesting the accounting centre of the Ministry of Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia to do this, and you can see this clearly in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D337. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to deal with another issue, namely the promotions in service. Mr. Skrbic, we heard some evidence about promotions in the Army of Republika Srpska, but so far we have not heard any evidence on promotions of generals. And that's what I would like to focus on right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see a document from the Defence 65 ter list, 00820D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, General, would you please tell me, based on which regulations and what type of promotions existed in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, as well as other regulations dealing with this in detail, such as orders on competencies that we saw earlier, promotions can be made from the rank of sergeant to warrant officer 2nd class, which are not commissioned officers, and then also promotions for officers from 2nd Lieutenant and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what kind of promotions are there? What types of promotions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm not sure I understood you well. There are so-called initial promotions --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initial promotions which are commissions. Somebody can be commissioned as a sergeant, and this is not really formally a promotion. This is when somebody receives their commission. It's a different matter. And then what else were you interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to the time-frame, to the period of time necessary for a promotion, how are promotions classified based on that? I don't want to lead you, but --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know how promotions are made from the rank of sergeant up to the rank of general, but I would need half an hour to describe all that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need for that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to competencies, who has powers to promote --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I was interested in. My question is as follows, and I hope Mr. Saxon will not object to this: Were there regular and extraordinary promotions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is the difference between these two terms? Why are there two kinds of promotions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to regular promotions, a person that is proposed for a promotion has to have a certain number of years, and the requirement is different for each rank. Normally they should have at least one year of service, and they also need to have certain educational qualifications for a promotion. All of these requirements were defined within the system when it comes to establishment positions. As for extraordinary or fast-track promotions, they are given to persons who achieve or do something very special extraordinary, or who do that over a certain period of time. They have a number of special achievements, and they can be promoted even if they do not meet the educational requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please comment on the document that we see on the screens. Just briefly, I think it's rather self-explanatory, this document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these promotions, and especially promotions to senior ranks, especially ranks of colonel and general were made on the occasion of a holiday, 28th of June. This is St. Vitus's Day and St. Vitus was the patron Saint of the Army of Republika Srpska. And also on the 9th of January, which is also a holiday of the patron Saint of the Army of Republika Srpska, and this is why we wanted everybody to submit their proposals, their candidacies, before a certain dead-line so that we would have time to prepare all that. Once it was approved, then orders were sent to -- by the Main Staff, and decrees were issued, and these orders or decrees on promotions were normally read at the command because brigades and units could be out there on the ground and not easily reachable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a brief question. Promotion to the rank of general in the Army of Republika Srpska. In addition to being read publicly in the unit, were such orders promoting somebody into rank of general also publicly announced, published?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a public enactment issued by the president of Republika Srpska who had powers to promote into rank of general. That would normally be announced in the main news programme which lasted between 7.30 until 8.00 p.m. prime-time television announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be admitted into evidence, and I suggest that we have our break after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D338.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we will stay with the topic of promotions. Can you describe for Their Honours what the procedure was like for promotions, particularly to the rank of general from the point when a proposal is made to the point where the president issues a decree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meetings of the collegium of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, discussions took place of all the promotions. In such situations, the collegium would sit in its extended form, meaning that corps commanders would be present. Special attention was paid to the promotions involving the rank of general. It was the commander of the Main Staff who took decisions on all the proposals from promotions who may have consulted with us. He would tell us to draft decrees and take them to the president who was the one vested with the power to issue a decree on promotions. Normally it would be me to take -- who would take such draft decrees to the president who, if in agreement with our proposal, would issue a decree promoting to the rank of general. Major-general would be the first to step, then the next would be lieutenant-general, the one above colonel-general, and then army general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up Defence 65 ter document 00056D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will be discussing this document very briefly. We looked at it during proofing. This is an order on the promotion of certain senior officers, and we'll see that it was signed by the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, and the date is the 7th of October, 1993. These are officers of lower rank, but the units involved are quite specific. The document is self-explanatory. Why was it Ratko Mladic who issued this order on promotions, and how does it tally with the order governing various competencies and powers that we looked at earlier?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is consistent with these powers. However, an important detail needs to be taken notice of, which is that the order was issued pursuant to Article 67 through to 74 of the Law on the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska and published, et cetera. I can't recall exactly if the order governing various powers was issued at roughly the same time. Nevertheless, there is not a single rank here which would be contrary to those powers, other than the fact that these lower ranks were subsequently transferred to the remit of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Law on the Service in the Armed Forces which was published in the SFRY "Official Gazette" is referred to and only subsequently is the RS law referred to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the other matter is this, we misunderstood each other. Were there specific units which were directly subordinated to the Main Staff and who had the power to decide on promotions related to these units?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listed these independent units attached to the Main Staff for you yesterday. For these units, promotions to ranks, whatever they may be, are issued by the commander of the Main Staff. And this is consistent with the order governing various powers because these are units that are immediately subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Do you want it under seal, sir? We are in open session. We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open. No need for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up Defence 65 ter 00065D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are still dealing with subject of promotions. Can you please comment on the document, tell us who signed it and what procedure this -- is involved in this document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the collegium of the commander of the Main Staff, the commander decided not to grant this request for the promotion of the individuals listed under 1 and 2, and we are here informing their units accordingly, which is clearly denoted by the fact that this is addressed by the military post 7590 Han Pijesak. I signed it, Petar Skrbic. It's a copy of my signature, but it is consistent with my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would such individuals and units be given the reasons why their requests or proposals were denied, or were they merely informed of the outcome?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would only be notified of the fact that their proposal was rejected. The reasons behind the decision are not given, as you can see in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D342. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, how important was a promotion in the Army of Republika Srpska? How important was it for the members of the VRS and the person being promoted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every promotion was very important for everybody in terms of the honour bestowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you said that the promotions were made public in front of the entire unit and when it came to the highest promotions, it was publicly announced on television, so how important was that fact, that it was announced publicly for everyone to hear?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to remind you that I said that neither the information nor the orders on promotion could be made public in front of the entire unit if that unit was out there on the ground on combat activities. At the Vlasic mount, a commander lined up his unit to publicly announce an order on promotion and a mortar grenade hit that line of soldiers killing a number of them. Following that, we banned any gatherings of that nature. However, commands did meet and read out orders on promotion publicly. The announcements, or rather, the orders on promotion were given personally to the person involved as soon as that became practicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 0061D, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 00061D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This morning we saw the order on competencies, defining competencies, so I would like you to comment on this document of General Mladic issued on the 26th of February, 1995. Why does it say implement again the order on defining competencies and so on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered this question this morning, but I will repeat it in one sentence. Here we can see that the order of the minister of defence on competencies of Ninkovic, which was only in the draft form, was never implemented, and this is why the commander is reminding us that this order needs to be implemented again, the order of Bogdan Subotic, the minister of defence that we saw this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D343. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not quite sure I understand, this document at paragraph 2 purports not to recognise any promotions that have not been proposed by the VRS. And I was going to be -- I was going to ask you what impact this has on promotions done by the minister, but now you are saying that this order says the order of Bogdan Subotic, the minister of defence that we saw this morning must be implemented again. Isn't it saying the opposite, that it should not be implemented, or am I missing something? Is it not refusing to recognise the minister's order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to item 3, which is that this document 23/20-1177 of the 23rd of December, 1994 is hereby set aside, so that minister Ninkovic at that point in time issued this order completely derogating the powers of the commander of the Main Staff when it comes to promotions. And this order mentioned in item 1, 21-59/92 dated 16th of June, regulates the power of the commander of the Main Staff when it comes to promotions. And I already said that he had powers from the rank of major to rank of lieutenant-colonel, whereas the minister of defence had powers from the rank of colonel up. Therefore, the commander hereby warns that we would not recognise the ranks that were not proposed by us, and we did not derogate the minister's powers to make promotions from the rank of colonel up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, how do you understand the term "verification?"

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Verification is a formal recognition of a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need a clarification. Formally by whom? Who is to recognise what? How do you understand this, tell us, please, so that we can analyse this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I always explain everything in my own words, so you don't need to worry about it. All promotions in the Army of Republika Srpska were actual real promotions. Following that, all those promotions were verified at the Army of Yugoslavia. Sometimes it took shorter, sometimes it took longer, sometime it took over a year for some generals for their rank to be verified. Why did this need to be verified? Because when it came to ranks, they were entitled to a pay increase. That could not be recognised in the Army of Yugoslavia if the rank had not been previously recognised by the Army of Yugoslavia as well. I'm trying to give you essential information here, and I don't think that anything more than this is required in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. You gave me an answer that seems to be fully clear to me. Now, what we and the Chamber are interested is this. What were the activities that your sector did in relation to this process of verification? Can you please focus on generals only because we already heard evidence about lower ranks. What did you have to do once the president of the republic promoted, say, you or some other general in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of promoted persons, especially generals, and nothing else other than the list was sent to the 30th personal centre or personnel administration with a proposal that these ranks be verified. Mr. Lukic, if I may add another sentence. Explanations or statement of reasons was written for all promotions, and a questionnaire on promotion was also filled. We did not send these questionnaires and statement of reasons to the 30th Personnel Centre. When I say "we" I'm referring to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were situations where the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I'm referring to the president of the republic because we are dealing with generals, whether they promoted a member of the VRS into a rank in the VJ without that person being previously promoted into that same rank in the VRS? Did you know of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that. However, I learned it only after the war and during our proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will discuss that case later, but outside of the case of General Ratko Mladic, do you know, when you came there all the way up until the end of the war while you headed that sector and while you were aware about promotions and verifications, did you know of any such cases where the matter was first resolved at the VJ and later on at the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of a case of General Radivoje Miletic, but there the time difference amounted to only two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at P1902, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see here decree of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Zoran Lilic dated the 16th of July, 1994, or rather, 16th of June, 1994, and this is an extraordinary promotion promoting Ratko Mladic to the rank of colonel-general, and this is the -- they are referring to the 30th Personnel Centre here. Does this date mean anything to you, 16th of June? Is that an important date for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption and perhaps I can be corrected, I'm not aware at this time that the Prosecution was notified that this document would be used. Were we, in fact notified? P1902. Because we have P1901 and 1903.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This could only be a typo. I was not interested in 1903, but 1901 and 1902 are two linked -- documents that are linked. I hope there will be no problems. 1901 has nothing to do with this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, if you could place on the record your gesture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise. Please carry on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does that mean? Does that mean you are satisfied with the explanation? You are happy to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to Mr. Saxon for his understanding, for understanding my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you heard the question, could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You asked about the 16th of June, 1994. 16th of June is the holiday of the Army of Yugoslavia. It was the date it was founded. And since it was known as the day of the army and it involved a number of celebrations and activities, then normally promotions were given on that day. So the same goes for this promotion, the 16th of June. Let me add this: In the Army of Yugoslavia, they used another date for announcing promotions, which was at the end of the year, but I think that it's a tradition they carried over from the Yugoslav People's Army. And why was that? Because in the Yugoslav People's Army, all promotions, especially those most important ones were done on the 22nd of December which was the day of the Yugoslav People's Army, it was their holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P1903, which is the document that is linked to the previous one. 1901 was a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have here the presidential decree of the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. The date is the 28th of June, 1994, and it involves an extraordinary promotion to the rank of colonel general of General Mladic, and it says that he was the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. So these two documents, when we put them in front of us, we see these difference of some two weeks in terms of the date, less than two weeks, 12 days, from the day he was promoted first in the Army of Yugoslavia and then in the VRS. Let me ask you this: The 28th of June, how is that a date important for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th of June is the day of the patron saint of the VRS. It is St. Vitus's Day. And there's the difference between the VRS and the VJ. The VJ did not have a patron saint and the VRS did. We in the VRS believed this to be -- or held this date to be one of the most joyous days because this was the day of our patron saint. And this is why most promotions were given on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, earlier we saw a document that was admitted into evidence showing the dead-lines for proposals for promotions. At this period of time, you were still at the Krajina Corps. Do you know whether a proposal was made for General Mladic to be promoted in the VRS, the promotion that he eventually did receive on St. Vitus's Day? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in lower subordinate units and in the army in general, just like in all armies, there are stories circulating about who is to be promoted into senior ranks, especially colonels and all the way up to generals. And I knew, my corps commander told me that General Mladic would most likely be promoted to the rank of colonel-general. But nobody knew for sure until the president issued a presidential decree, but people were commenting on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So had he not been promoted in the VJ, or rather, had his promotion not been verified in the VJ on the 16th of June, when was the first next occasion it could have been done before this promotion that was made on the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that in the VJ the generals from the VJ were promoted in December, and then the next occasion was for the ones who were verified, so that could have been done in December. I have another piece of information that I can tell you by your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? Up until my proofing session with Mr. Lukic, I did not know at all that this rank was verified for General Mladic, nor have I ever asked him about it. He didn't like to discuss such topics with us, when it came to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to say, Mr. Lukic, it would be odd for me to call what happened on the 16th of June verification. When you verify, you verify something that has happened. Nothing had happened by the 16th of June. What happened in the VRS happened on the 28th of June, so there couldn't be -- there was a promotion, it was not a verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that sense, Your Honour, you are quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, from your personal experience and as an individual who dealt with the issue of moral guidance and morale, when were you promoted to the rank of major-general within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of major-general on the 23rd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the rank verified in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you showed me that document from my personnel file as well, but I can't remember the date. I only remember that it was in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, Mr. Skrbic, while Mr. Lukic is looking through his book, what saint day is the 23rd of June? What patron is recognised on the 23rd of June? I thought promotions take place on patron's day on the VRS. You were promoted on the 23rd of June. I'm asking is that a patron's day and who is the patron on the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be my pleasure to explain this to you. My promotion bears the date of the 23rd of June, but it was pronounced on the patron saint's day, i.e., on the 28th of June. The decree does not necessarily have to bear the date of the 28th of June, but it was on the 28th of June that General Petar Skrbic and other generals who were on the list together with him, on that occasion that they were formally promoted. You see, I had activities in Bijeljina as well where festivities were organised in my honour and this too took place on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have the time to go through your personnel file fully, but what it says with regard to your promotions, what it mentions as the date when you were promoted to the rank of major-general in the Army of Yugoslavia is the 27th of December, 1995. Now, what did the verification received from the Army of Yugoslavia, the verification of a promotion to a certain rank mean to you as an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was on the 23rd of June, 1995 that I became a general and that's something that I knew rationally, but I can't say that it didn't have a meaning for me emotionally as well in view of the rank that I received and the fact that it was verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the verification of ranks issued by the Army of Yugoslavia, were they published, were they at all discussed amongst officers in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, one of the interpreters said something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Could all unnecessary microphones be switched off, because in the French booth we hear English a lot from somebody's headphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, so much. We will do that. Sorry, you were saying something, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said something which wasn't entered in the transcript. You said you made a distinction between the public at large and the officers themselves. Can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, nothing was published, and the general public in Yugoslavia was not privy to this. I drew this distinction because it was, of course, natural that we should discuss it. Even after verifications were made, the entitlements were late in arriving, so of course, that's why the officers would discuss these matters, but they were not discussed in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We discussed the meetings called collegium in the Main Staff. Can you tell us how did these collegia of the Main Staff work, and I mean the inner collegium. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer the question from the perspective of the specialist line I dealt with. I would inform the commander and tell him General, sir, we have quite a lot of material to discuss at the impending meeting. I have prepared the material, can you tell me when we can schedule a session of the collegium. He would inform me about it and at such meetings, whenever promotions were discussed, we would have an extended composition, which would include corps commanders, rank and file, because they had to be heard and their proposals had to be heard as well. There were two books of records, I'll really make this answer as short as possible. There was one book of records, which I kept as the chief of the sector for organisation affairs, and the other book of records kept by the commander. He would enter on the right-hand side of the book in response to a certain question yes or no, and that was the book that was used as reference, his commander's book of notes. That book was used as the basis for all the documents that my sector produced. These were quite large books of records. It would so happen that we wouldn't be able to discuss all the points, so we had to leave them for later. I may have even bore the commander sometime with these affairs, but that's what these meetings of the collegium were like. Of course, the collegium also discussed other issues. I can -- I'm open to discussing those as well. I only answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I have another general question, which I don't believe I put yesterday. From the point you became a member of the staff and by that token a member of the collegium, did the collegium meet regularly during the war, and if so, at which intervals, and how far between, let's put it that way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only after the war that the meetings of the collegium of the commander would take place regularly. During the war, it depended on the situation, whenever practicable. I even told you that during the war when some personnel matters were discussed, meetings had to be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave us a specific answer, but can you be more general. You said as practicable but can you give us a more specific answer, although I understand that you can't be too specific?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part of the Main Staff and of the collegium which was stationed in Crna Rijeka had the opportunity to meet on a daily basis. I don't know that they did, but General Djukic and I who were in -- who were away from that particular location, we would normally told -- attend monthly meetings and then that would be, of course, in addition to the issues that I discussed. In certain periods the meetings would take place in shorter intervals as the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have been hearing a term in this case, and I am sure that it will arise again. Have you ever heard of the term personnel council, and if you did, can you tell us what it stands for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of the term which stems from the Law on the Service in the Armed Forces of the SFRY which stipulates that persons participating in discussions at the personnel -- in the personnel council have a vote of parity and the matters discussed normally concern personnel. In other words, if somebody was promoted, or rather, if someone was eligible for promotion, the commander could not just make a promotion without the personnel council, but the personnel council did not exist in the VRS. Your Honour, I have myself seen certain documents, and I'm sure you will, where an individual was a member of the -- or wrote the term personnel council, but I can tell you for a fact that personnel council did not exist in the VRS. We did discuss matters. We were consulted. Our votes were taken into consideration, but they were not decisive. It was the commander who would take the decision on an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I keep repeating myself, but I would like you to focus on the period you became part of the Main Staff in August of 1994. From that point on, had you ever heard of the so-called co-ordination meetings of the three army, or had you previously heard of co-ordination meetings of three armies, and had you ever participated in anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard of such meetings, but I had never taken part in them, nor were they held as of my arrival on the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move to a different subject now, which is interesting because it is mentioned in the indictment and related to your sector. Did your sector have as part of its competence any sort of participation in the training of officers of the VRS? And may I just intervene because this is a very important term, there's training and education, and I'm asking about education specifically, not training, and I think the interpreters -- can you, in fact, explain for us, did your sector take part in any training, that's also important?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not participate in training, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in what sense was your sector involved in educating the personnel of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The education of VRS personnel at various levels was one of the core activities of my sector which was titled, you know how, I don't want to repeat that lengthy title again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just make a correction. In answer to my question at page 51, line 3, the witness said the -- that they did not participate in training, no. I don't want to exclude the possibility that some other sector was involved in training. I understood Mr. Skrbic to answer in the sense that his sector did not participate in the training of VRS members and can ask him now to answer the question again, did your sector participate in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question specifically says that. He has answered to your question. Your question was, did your sector take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, I apologise. It is quite clear then. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did there exist military schools in Republika Srpska, and if so, when and where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war in Republika Srpska there existed the commissioned and non-commissioned officers school as part of the centre of high military schools Rajko Bajic in Banja Luka. The education of non-commissioned officers lasted a year and for the commissioned officers a year as well which was actually a shortened term with a view to ensuring the joining of officers in the VRS as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who provided funding for the schooling?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school was financed by the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... when it's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of the schooling, would the individuals be conferred a rank, and who was it who actually, as you put it, confers a rank upon them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-commissioned officers would be given the rank of sergeant by the Ministry of Defence and the attendees of the school for commissioned officers for their promotion to the rank of second lieutenant, that promotion would be made by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another short question, these non-commissioned officers and commissioned officers once promoted to their respective ranks, did they have anything to do with the 30th Personnel Centre and the payroll from the FRY and the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
