utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the break we discussed education in the military schools of Republika Srpska. I'd like the following information to be recorded. How many attendees were there in a class of students in the school for commissioned and non-commissioned officers in Republika Srpska during the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These schools had four classes in all, a class would complete its schooling in a term of one year. And roughly there were from 50 to 100 students in each. And this applies to both schools. I'm not really familiar with the precise figures, but I don't think it went over 100 per class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the citizens of Republika Srpska during the war attend the military schools of Army of Yugoslavia, to what extent was your sector involved in it, and did you have any information about it all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The admissions exams for the high school, the associate degree military schools, and the military academy were advertised in Republika Srpska. The Main Staff of the VRS wanted as many citizens as possible to apply for such admissions exams, but we could have no impact on it other than encourage people to join these schools. Citizens applied for these exams for military schools of the Army of Yugoslavia depending on their wishes and abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you are referring to these schools, I suppose you are referring to the military academy and the non-commissioned officers schools?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of ranks would they be promoted to at the end of these schools, and what did that have to do with the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens who sat the admissions exams for secondary military schools would upon completion of their secondary schooling continue in the military academy. Those who applied for secondary military schools and graduated from those would be promoted to the rank of sergeant. Those who graduated from the military academy of the Army of Yugoslavia would be promoted to the initial rank of 2nd lieutenant in a ceremony held in Belgrade. And that's an officer's, commissioned officer's rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What would happen with them next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may answer that question, Mr. Skrbic, I'll ask mine later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please remind me of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What would happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is what would happen with them next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those who had left Republika Srpska for their schooling would return to Republika Srpska, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was at page 53 line 12, Mr. Lukic says -- asked you a question, did the citizens of Republika Srpska during the war attend the military schools of the Army of Yugoslavia, to what extent was your sector involved in it, and did you have any information about it, although it's a very long compound question. And you then said that admissions exams for high school, associate degree for military school and military academy were advertised, when these people who were -- these citizens who were attending these schools, they were attending the schools in the Army of Yugoslavia. My question to you is, were there none attending schools in the Republika Srpska? Or were there no schools in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, save for the schools that I referred to, which operated on a shortened programme, there were people attending these schools in the Army of Yugoslavia which had a full term and full curriculum. Of course we could not exert any sort of influence on citizens who wanted to go to study in the schools of the Army of Yugoslavia because it was a different country. It was Mr. Milan Gvero who was in charge of this sector specifically and who promoted military schooling to the public at large. That was his role. We, for our part, could not encourage anyone directly to go and attend military schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how long was the full term of schooling? You've told us one year when you talked about the VRS schools, but -- and the full term in the Yugoslav schools, how long was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The full term for officers was eight years of schooling, four years of secondary military school and four years of the military academy. For non-commissioned officers, the schooling lasted four years in the secondary military school in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may he proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of the two years, or rather, through to the end of the war starting from mid-1994 when you took up the position of the chief of sector, according to your information and to the best of your recollection, how many such future VRS servicemen were educated and schooled in the Army of Yugoslavia? How many, let's say, per generation, per class?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the information concerning the military academy. In the beginning of the war up to 50 people had graduated from the academy. In the course of the war, that's to say 1993, 1994, and 1995, the number dwindled. In 1994, I took over in Belgrade 51 non-commissioned officers and 28 officers with the rank of 2nd lieutenant who had graduated from the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was entered correctly, your answer. Can you say 1994, how many non-commissioned officers did you -- or rather, the 2nd lieutenant officers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 31. It says 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 51 non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that's an error, Your Honour. There was mention of 2nd Lieutenant Officers who had graduated from the academy, whereas he said that he was not charged with dealings with non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question on this topic, Mr. Skrbic. Do you know if during the war at the time when you took up your position in the Main Staff some of the members of the VRS went to attend command staff schools, specialised schools, or the school of national defence of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was that those who had graduated from the military academy need not attend post-graduate schools because the war itself was the best of schooling. So during the war we did not send a single individual to attend any of these schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have completed this topic now. I would like to briefly analyse an institution that we haven't dealt with so far which is the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska. What sort of body is this, and who does it comprise? Can you first answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Supreme Command of the Republika Srpska or Supreme Command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command of Republika Srpska, I think that's the proper title. I think so. I'm not sure either. The witness will tell us.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will tell you now exactly what its title is. This was defined in a law published in the "Official Gazette." I had occasion to review the law which was present in other cases as well. It is called the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska. The armed forces of Republika Srpska during the war comprise the Army of Republika Srpska and the MUP, which stands for the Ministry of the Interior. The Supreme Command is composed of the supreme commander, i.e., the president of the republic, who by virtue of this position is the supreme commander. Next, the minister of the interior, minister of defence -- I'm sorry, I seem to have lost track of my answer. Minister of defence and nobody else. From the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, nobody was a member of the Supreme Command. Let me add that the Supreme Command was co-opted by the president of the republic and the vice-president. These were, and can I tell their names? Dr. Nikola Koljevic and madam Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the president of the Assembly take part in the work of the Supreme Command, do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that I'm in a dilemma here perhaps. I can't answer the question because I'm not certain. It can be reviewed in the document I referred to in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not go into any further detail because we hope to call a witness who can discuss this topic. I will move on to a different subject. There is another aspect of the service that is to say termination of service and retirement that we will discuss at a later point, but I would like to discuss an event now. Mr. Skrbic, you joined the Main Staff in the summer of 1994. Does the plan of the Contact Group mean anything to you? Can you tell us, do you know anything about the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of the plan and the proposal of the Contact Group which consisted of you know who was something I wasn't familiar with. I was familiar with the map proposed by the contact group, and I do recall that we discussed this issue at several meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, what the position of the political leadership of the Republika Srpska was in relation to the adoption of the plan of the Contact Group? You also say that you discussed the issue, do you know what the specific issue was, what the proposal was, was it acceptable to you? Can you briefly tell us what you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object first of all to the compound nature of the question. Second of all, he has indicated in his evidence, he says the contents of the plan he wasn't familiar with, so I have two objections to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to make you aware of that second part, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, it is stated in the transcript that you said that you are not familiar with the contents of the plan. But you said that you discussed something at the meeting of the Main Staff. Can you tell us what did you discuss and what the position of the Main Staff was? My apologies, I'm not focused enough. Can you tell us what it involved.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in no uncertain terms that I was familiar with the map proposed by the Contact Group. On this map, Bosnia-Herzegovina looked like leopard skin, fragmented and made into little parts. And this was basis enough for us to discuss it. And it was precisely because of the map that we didn't need to look at the contents at all. It was on the basis of a map that we discussed whether the plan should be accepted or not. It was precisely because of the way the map appeared that the military leadership of Republika Srpska and the political leadership, that is to say the president and other members of the government did not accept the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the decision taken by the authorities and by the Assembly of Republika Srpska regarding that plan when it was discussed in those circles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hasn't just told us that? He said it was on the basis of the map that the political leadership and the military leadership did not accept the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to suggest, but did the Assembly make a decision on some referendum? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But I have to be quite specific now, we know that the Assembly adopted the decision to schedule a referendum, and then we from the Main Staff of the VRS regulated technical issues as to how members of the VRS could vote at the referendum. I have to tell you that I am not familiar with the results of the voting at the referendum, but given that the plan of the Contact Group was rejected, I would say that authorities must have take into account the outcome of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the position of the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia when it came to the acceptance of the plan?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. They wanted the plan to be accepted unconditionally and without reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you and members of the Main Staff have any direct contacts with the members of the VJ in relation to the plan?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you describe when that was, how, and with whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we remember some dates so well that we can never forget them. You have seen here that sometimes I answer questions without being able to remember some of the details. However, I remember very well that a meeting was held in Crna Rijeka. It was a sunny day, the meeting was held outside in open air and the meeting was between the delegation of the VRS led by General Perisic, and the inner collegium of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. And this is what we discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter says it was a meeting and the inner collegium of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS and this is -- wait a minute, a meeting between the delegation of the VRS led by General Perisic. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said, but I don't see that it was reflected here that it was on the 12th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You hadn't mentioned the date yet. But what I do want to know is that are you saying General Perisic was leading a delegation of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No, no, I apologise. Not the VRS, the VJ. Army of Yugoslavia. I almost got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: General Perisic was leading the delegation of the VJ and that delegation, who was it meeting in Crna Rijeka? Which delegation was it meeting or what group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the members of the inner collegium of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, I can give you the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are going back to what we have touched upon two days ago. The procedure is such that I first want this one document which is from the notebook of Ratko Mladic to be discussed with the witness. It is not on the 65 ter list of the Defence. It has been marked as doc 1D12-0009. We have received the CLSS official translation of the document from this meeting. The meeting is with General Perisic on the 12th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, sir. You have raised a point here which I think even before you carry on talking about that document we would need to hear the response of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Obviously we have no objection to the diary being used. I understand, however, that CLSS translation, I was informed before I came into court, that it was just received within the hour. So we have not had an opportunity to review it and we would ask that it be MFI'd, the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you. I think that by tomorrow the OTP will be able to verify this. Could we now analyse this document with the witness, please. I will now give the 65 ter designation of the Defence. It's 03334. 03334.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, please, you have already mentioned, and we will see as we go through these pages that your name is mentioned here. Can we just go over some pages of this document. The first thing we see is the date, the 12th of August, 1994, KM Friday. What does KM stand for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says "meeting with general." I will read the first part --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can I put a question. I apologise, a question to the Trial Chamber regarding such documents, and I put the same question to you earlier on. Your Honours, may I put a question to you, it's about the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may. In proofing with Mr. Lukic, I asked to see the original based on which copies of these notebooks were made because I would like to, and I also see that you want everything to be as specific and accurate as possible, I wanted to see the original of at least one notebook. I didn't have to see all notebooks but in order to establish authenticity I wanted to see at least one, even though this handwriting is rather familiar to me, but I wanted to see at least one original of these notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I give a comment concerning what the witness just said to the Trial Chamber? I wanted to warn the Chamber that I have around spoken to Mr. Saxon regarding this. When I had proofing with this witness, I wrote this down in the proofing note and then Mr. Saxon called me up asking for an explanation, and I conveyed to him what Mr. Skrbic had told me during proofing. We, as Defence, do not challenge the authenticity of the documents, and we put them on our 65 ter list. Mr. Saxon explained to me that the OTP, as an institution, takes very good care of this document and that any contact with the document could create what Mr. Saxon described to me as even DNA problems. I would like to know whether during some break, Mr. Skrbic could be shown this document. I don't know whether the OTP can help us with this. But we are not going to either challenge or prove the authenticity of this document via Mr. Skrbic. For us this document is authentic. And in that respect, Mr. Saxon told me that they were not going to put any questions to Mr. Skrbic concerning these matters that are of concern to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will regulate that with Mr. Lukic at the appropriate time. I understand that colour copies of these documents have been made, that they are available for the witness to examine. They are almost perfect reproductions of the documents themselves. There are reasons why the originals are inaccessible at the moment, it relates to the contamination that Mr. Lukic discussed with Mr. Saxon. So I will regulate that with the Court's permission where Mr. Lukic. I think we've resolved the issue in terms of the authenticity, it's not an issue in this case with these documents according to the Defence. And I don't want to run the risk of contaminating evidence that could have other purposes, could be affected by DNA and contamination from sources, other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must confess, you gentleman are speaking above me. The witness would like to see the original. A colour copy is not an original. He might as well look at what we are looking at the screen. Where you are above me is where you talk about contamination by DNA. Now, these documents were taken from the house of Mr. Mladic by police, handled by them, given to the Prosecution, handled by the Prosecution. The Prosecution made transcripts into Latin script, passed on the originals with the Latin scripts to CLSS, the documents are handled by the CLSS, there's a lot of contamination that has taken place here. I just want to know what this contamination is that can be brought about by Mr. Skrbic if he was to look at these documents in the presence of his counsel and in the presence of somebody from the Prosecution if somebody from the Prosecution must verify that Mr. Skrbic does nothing to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've not been dealing with this particular issue. It's been dealt with by a team of people in my office, including Mr. Saxon. He is in the best position to give Your Honour an answer to this question and enlighten you further as to the contamination issue and the potential issue. I'm not. If we could defer this issue and this matter then we will offer Your Honours a proper explanation to what our concerns are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I look forward to that explanation. Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, I guess you heard what they are saying about your question that you raised. You wanted to see the original. Mr. Harmon and Mr. Lukic will try to sort the problem out and see how best they can give you something that you can look at. Now I have a question for you. Are you able to testify further on this document without having seen the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would like to see at least one notebook of the original. I don't see -- I don't have to see all of it, and I don't even have to touch it with my hand. I'm very pleased about what you said. I saw photocopies in colour but they are still just photocopies as you said. I apologise for taking up your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not taking up our time, Mr. Skrbic. We are here to hear you and we must hear you. That's our job. Thank you for saying that, and I want to underline what you said. You don't even want to touch them, you just want to see them. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I will cover this document the same way we did it two days ago. I will ask you about the fact, especially since you were present at this meeting and you remember it. I'm now reading the first portion. "General Perisic, it pleases me that we are here among you. We have passed through the blockade incognito and we are here, A to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can I interrupt you, I guess you are going to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I want to believe that it goes beyond this first page? Is this all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The document has some ten pages. It's a large document. 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My worry is now you are starting to read it instead of putting it here for us to read it and then you can ask your questions, because we can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I'm not going to read all of it, just.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree. Only some sequences is what I'm going to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I have just read out what's on the first page where it says, "we have passed through the blockade incognito," what does this pertain to? How did you understand this if this is indeed what General Perisic said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the niceties as uttered by General Perisic at the beginning of the meeting. I don't know why they had to do it incognito. Maybe somebody had forbidden them from going across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a blockade at the time imposed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia against the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Mr. Lukic for reminding me. There are things that I simply cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please, both in English and in B/C/S. I think they correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here it says under C that we need to agree on how to proceed from here. Then a couple of lines down, I don't know if you can see it on the screen in the original. The English is quite legible, but do you see what General Perisic says about the position of the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Can you read that? I can also put the Serbian text in Latin script.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can read this handwriting quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did that during proofing too. From this bullet point where it says the stand of the FRY leadership, I have read everything until the end of the page. Does it look like those were the words of General Perisic during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic conveyed to us the position of the FRY leadership with these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle it says the position of the FRY, if the plan is accepted, they will continue assisting as they have so far or better. If the plan is not accepted than a series of measures will be implemented. Some have already been implemented. What did they mean by this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant by this is that the border was closed in every sense, the border between the FRY and the Republika Srpska at the Drina River and in other places. If the plan was not accepted, then further and I would add, drastic measures were to follow. That the embargo would be expanded on to military personnel as well, that all contacts and links would be terminated, and that Republika Srpska would be placed in a cage. This was added by me, but I'm doing that because I was present at the meeting, and I listened to what was said there. This is a matter for -- added by me. There was no mention of cage at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, before Mr. Lukic goes on, there is that sentence that says, "the position of the FRY, if the plan is accepted, they will continue assisting as they have so far or better." Who are the "they" here? Is that the FRY? The they who will continue assisting. Who are those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They is the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The information contained therein is self-explanatory, I believe. These are bullets standing for the words uttered by General Perisic. That's right. The page is correct. Perhaps the fourth or fifth line reads: "A conflict has erupted between the policies of the FRY and the RS. The policy of the FRY favours the protection of something general (the national being of the Serbian people), while the policy of the RS favours the protection of something specific. I think that both a struggle for power and the personal interests of individuals are involved here." And then I'm interested in what follows next. "In order to avoid divisions, the message of the FRY leadership to you as soldiers is: To perform tasks." In English it says police tasks, whereas I'm convinced that the term in Serbian doesn't say that. I was unable to decipher the word myself, but I don't know if General Skrbic can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want to take the stand, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm clear on the continuation of the sentence, but the word itself is not something that I can make out at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask the witness. Unless you want to swap places with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Skrbic, can you make out what it says there? To perform tasks, and can this be enlarged a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I start my answer -- in giving my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Lukic showed me this document, I read and reread the word a dozen times, and I could not make myself believe that what it really says is police, but unfortunately, it does seem that it says so. I can't decipher the word. Knowing the state of affairs at the time, I don't think this should in fact be police here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this bit be zoomed in on -- that's the middle part of the page, the bit that is in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see the word clearly, but I can't decipher it. However, what follows next is: In other words, to reject the authority or refuse obedience to the ERS leadership, this is something that I can see clearly, and I can read clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I don't understand is the following paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the 14th of August, 1994, they want to form a flying Chetnik corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was about to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now read out in Serbian, and I hope that the interpreters can follow, and then General Skrbic can explain to us what General Perisic meant by this. "They are announcing a bloody September and on the 14th of August, 1994 in Kostajnica, they want to form a flying Chetnik corps, to which many of those who were unstable or were retired on any grounds have gone. They are trying to find a corps for the soldiers and officers in all three armies. There are particular many such persons, around 20 to 30 per cent in the MUP of Serbia." Have I read this accurately, General?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is that General Perisic is referring here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic is conveying to us the intelligence that he received from the competent sector in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. In view of the fact that General Perisic was aware of us not supporting the Chetnik army, when I say "us," I mean the VRS and the Main Staff, he is conveying to us something that may be an accurate piece of information, that a Chetnik corps was in the making, that would include various Chetniks from various armies. The Army of Republika Srpska was constantly opposed to Chetnik units and did not allow for their establishment. This piece of information conveyed by General Perisic was told with the intention of letting us know that on the 14th of August, 1994, we may expect para-military formations to be set up in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page, please. Both in the B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we are going to tender this document, we are not going to keep reading these paragraphs, the witness can read them for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. If I observe any discrepancies between what I'm reading and the translation, well, I hope we won't have any problems what that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you see there it says SM, and from what I can make out it says message from him and then a colon and several bullet points. Can you read that, please, and I'll have a couple of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the bullet points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can see that the translation service has already marked something in the English translation which I wanted to ask the witness about, but I have to since we don't have that in the B/C/S because we have SM, and we don't have the text in brackets explaining what it stands for. But can I ask you, whose message was conveyed here by General Perisic, who is SM?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be concluded reliably that SM stands for Slobodan Milosevic, and the translation here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you have just read here, does it reflect the words uttered by General Perisic at the meeting as you remember them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. This has remained etched in my memory just as a lightening when it hits the tree and halves it, just as that tree remains always in halves, the same way I can never forget these words conveyed by Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was written here in no uncertain terms that Slobodan Milosevic was asking from you to reject the authority of the leadership of Republika Srpska. This is something that General Perisic told you on this occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And he asked another individual to convey this message to us instead of coming there personally to tell us as much. And I'm very sorry about that. Let me tell you what I feel about it. Why didn't he appear in person and tell us what he had to say instead of using other individuals to convey his messages?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will later on have an opportunity to hear out what your reactions were to these words. I would now like to now see who the participants involved were, and let's take it page by page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the next page to see who took the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we'd like you to tell us who is who because this isn't annotated in the diary. The first thing that is written at the top is General R. Milovanovic. Do you know who this individual is and which army he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know -- this is General Ratko Milovanovic, assistant chief for logistics of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and he accompanied Mr. Perisic. In English you can add the word Ratko. Ratko Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Below it is written General Dimitrijevic. Who is he, and what position did he have, and do you recall him being at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic, his first name Aleksandar, was the chief of the administration for security of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. He was present at the meeting having arrived there together with General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move two pages ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says at the top, Discussion by members of the GS VRS. The first individual mentioned is General Milovanovic and we said that he was Chief of the General Staff, and you explained his role fully yesterday. I would like you to comment on one point made somewhere in the middle. It says "Yugoslavia's stand," do you see that? "In my opinion is an ultimatum," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if we accept the plan, we can have a confederation, or if it is a no, then that we will have a blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see, Your Honours, there is a certain discrepancy between what I was reading and the translation because the word [B/C/S spoken] in the B/C/S was interpreted, is missing in translation, and I can read it quite clearly, but I will be going through the document carefully once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I read just now, do you recall these being the words uttered by General Milovanovic, and do you recall this roughly being the tenor of his address?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer this question can I make one point, Your Honours. In these notebooks you will most likely be coming across the abbreviation NS, which stands for the Chief of Staff, that was General Milovanovic. But that was the informal title. His formal title was the chief of the sector of operations and training, just as my full title -- he was the chief of sector for operations and staff affairs. So that was his title. What is written here accurately reflects his position, and I believe that he was the most articulate, clear, and resolute in the presentation of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page and see what General Milovanovic had to say. Your Honours, I will read that sentence out loud because I think that the interpreters in the booth are following me well, and it is very clear for me that the transcript is accurate when it comes to this particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "You are asking us to reject authority of our leadership. This leadership was elected by the people, and they are what they are. I cannot reject authority of such a leadership because you did not reject authority of your leadership either." Do you remember these words of General Milovanovic, and were they, indeed, as reflected in this document, and if so, what did they mean at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember these words well, and perhaps this is the portion that remained best etched in my memory. I didn't really try to remember the things that were of a general nature. So General Milovanovic very clearly explained his position, namely that we were not going to turn our backs to the leadership of Republika Srpska because we considered it the official leadership of our republic and they became -- they were given that authority and legitimacy at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we see the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, is it then your testimony that there was no agreement within the delegation led by General Perisic? You indicated that General Milovanovic came as part of Mr. Perisic's delegation. He seems to be differing -- his stand is differing from the stand of Mr. Perisic, or am I misunderstanding again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but you are misunderstanding this. The first Milovanovic I mentioned, his first name is Ratko. That Milovanovic arrived with General Perisic. As for the other Milovanovic who has the same last name, his first name is Manojlo, and he is at the staff of the VRS. It just so happened that they had the same last names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for clearing that. Thank you so much. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see General Djukic. We already know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we had the right page. Please go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lead you, but General Djukic was a member of your Main Staff; right? Chief for logistics. I don't think Mr. Harmon will object to me saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know who General Djukic is, but I don't know if this General Djukic was the General Djukic who was in attendance at this particular meeting, and I think it's important rather than lead the witness, to ask this witness who he is and perhaps this witness will identify him as the same General Djukic, it may be a different General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just give a general warning, Mr. Lukic, about leading questions. Even if they are not objected against, you know what the effect they have, they have the effect of lessening the probative value of your witness's testimony. Even without suggesting that he not credible, he is credible, but the fact that you put words into his mouth, that's what happens when his testimony gets assessed that this man was not testifying, he was being told answers and what probative value can you put on this. It is in your own interest that you don't lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I make mistakes unconsciously, I am certainly guilty, but sometimes I'm doing this in order to speed up the proceedings, and there is no need to do that. I was just thinking that there are some things that are so familiar that we can speed through, but you are quite right, Your Honours, I should do it by the book so that it can be evaluated properly. I will follow your instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honours, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've heard Mr. Lukic asking me who is General Djukic, but I don't want to interrupt him and answer immediately. I'm following the transcript and I'm waiting to make sure that the interpretation is recorded before I start answering, but it was completely clear to me that he asked me who General Djukic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Skrbic, and you're doing the right thing, and we are taking no issue with what you are doing. I'm just sort of trying to say to Mr. Lukic there are certain procedures that we got to follow. Just like you had some procedures you had to follow in the army, like unity of command, that's the one lesson I've learned about the army, I'm getting there, but there are also procedures here, and he knows them, so that's what I'm trying to say. Thank you so much. Okay. You can tell us who Mr. Djukic is -- General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His first name is Djordje, and he was assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS for logistics. You call it the sector for logistics here. He attended the meeting, and where it says "General Djukic," it refers to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on what is in this rectangle here where

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please, to see who is mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says Lieutenant-Colonel Koranovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In answer it says Koranovic -- in English it says Koranovic. Please tell us who this is.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Jovica Karanovic worked at the security administration of the Main Staff of the VRS at the sector for intelligence and security affairs of the VRS. He also attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see that the transcript reflects Koranovic as the translation, but it's not Koranovic, it should be Karanovic. K-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then underneath it it says, Puk Skrbic. I have to ask you, who is this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is me. At the time I was Pukovnik, a colonel, and I was about to take over the new duty. I came to the Main Staff on the 27th of July, and I took over my new duty on the 15th of August. However, I attended this meeting, as I have explained to you earlier. This is meeting that remained etched in my memory and where I took the floor. Not everything I said is reflected here in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since what witness Skrbic said takes up almost an entire page of this document and I see what time it is, I suggest that we stop for the day and then turn to the words of Mr. Skrbic tomorrow. I have to add another issue. I don't know whether you will ever put this question to me, but you are probably wondering how long witness Skrbic is going to testify. Initially we said eight to ten hours, but given the documents and given this particular document, I expect to continue tomorrow for the whole day. This is the only witness who will be coming from the Main Staff, and I think that he needs to be given this much time and you will see tomorrow from the topics that I will cover with him that they are all deserving topics that need to be heard viva voce in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we remove this document from the screen, please. Thank you so much. May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Skrbic, again it's the end of the day for us today. The next court must come and sit. Again I remind you you are not supposed to discuss the case with anybody, in particular not with your Defence counsel until you are excused from the stand. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow again, same courtroom, 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.
